6._section_summary: This introduction section discusses the evolution of body image research towards positive body image, particularly body appreciation. It highlights the distinct nature of positive body image predictors compared to negative body image. The section outlines the aim of the present study, which is to integrate body appreciation into models of body image and eating behavior, examining interpersonal and intrapersonal variables as predictors and body appreciation as a mediator for outcomes like depressive symptoms and intuitive eating. The study draws upon insights from previous qualitative research by Wood-Barcalow et al. (2010) and Frisén and Holmqvist (2010) to inform its model variables.

2._section_summary: This abstract describes a study that developed and investigated a model of positive body image, positioning body appreciation as a mediator. The model was tested with 249 college women, showing that restrictive/critical caregiver eating messages, attachment anxiety, and discrepancy perfectionism inversely predicted body appreciation, while order perfectionism positively predicted it. Body appreciation, in turn, positively predicted intuitive eating and mediated the relationship between several predictors and intuitive eating. This section describes a single study.

3._section_summary: This section describes the participants of a single study, consisting of 249 college women from a university in the Midwestern U.S. The mean age was 19.1 years, and 86.3% identified as White/Caucasian. The sample included students from various academic years, with a majority being first-year students.

4._section_summary: This section details the various measures used in the current study, including the Body Appreciation Scale (BAS), Caregiver Eating Messages Scale (CEMS), Experiences in Close Relationships Scale (ECRS), Almost Perfect Scale-Revised (APS-R), Beck Depression Inventory-II (BDI-II), and Intuitive Eating Scale (IES). It also describes how Body Mass Index (BMI) was assessed. The section refers to 'the current sample' throughout, indicating a single study.

5._section_summary: This section details the procedure for a single study. It describes that all procedures were approved by the university's IRB, and participants were recruited from female introductory psychology students via a research board in the Department of Psychology. Participants completed measures in a classroom setting, with the purpose of investigating body attitudes, personality characteristics, and eating behavior, ensuring anonymity and counterbalancing measures.

6._extracted_caption: Table 1 Means (Standard deviations) and correlations among measures and BMI.
6._section_summary: This section details the testing of a hypothesized model, including controlling for BMI and justifying the sample size of N=249. It describes the statistical analysis using Mplus, the fit indices (CFI, SRMR, RMSEA), and the iterative process of examining, trimming, and revising the structural model based on modification indices. The final model, presented in Fig. 2, accounted for significant percentages of variance in body appreciation, intuitive eating, depressive symptoms, and perfectionism variables.

7._section_summary: This section presents the conclusion of a study involving college women, focusing on a model that investigates interpersonal and intrapersonal links to body appreciation and its connection to intuitive eating. Body appreciation is highlighted as a central mediational variable, accounting for links from restrictive/critical caregiver eating messages, attachment anxiety, and discrepancy perfectionism to intuitive eating. The study also found that body appreciation did not predict unique variance in depressive symptoms, suggesting it is distinct from negative body image.

The number of participants (N = 249) exceeded the minimum 5:1 participants-to-parameter ratio needed to confidently examine a model (Bentler, 1990). In this study, a total of 225 participants were needed as there were 45 parameters (25 variable-to-variable paths, 10 standard error paths to the model variables, five BMI-to-variable paths, and five BMI standard error paths) in Fig. 1. Our sample size also exceeded the N 
 200 recommendation for complex models (Weston & Gore, 2006).
6._section_summary: This section details the test of a hypothesized model, starting with the justification of the sample size (N = 249) and the statistical methods used (Mplus, CFI, SRMR, RMSEA). It describes the examination of an initial structural model, the subsequent trimming of nonsignificant paths, and a final revision based on modification indices to achieve a more parsimonious and better-fitting model. The final model's significant standardized path coefficients are presented in Fig. 2, with body appreciation variance notably accounted for by several factors.

8._section_summary: This section details a mediation analysis examining body appreciation as a mediator between discrepancy perfectionism, order perfectionism, attachment anxiety, restrictive/critical caregiver eating messages, and intuitive eating. The methodology involved using Shrout and Bolger's (2002) bootstrap procedures with Mplus to generate 1000 bootstrap samples and bias-corrected confidence intervals for indirect effects. The results indicated that body appreciation fully mediated the link from discrepancy perfectionism to intuitive eating and partially mediated the links from attachment anxiety and restrictive/critical caregiver eating messages to intuitive eating, while the indirect effect from order perfectionism was not significant.
